The alchemists' name for the whole labour of transmutation, from first blackness to the perfected Stone — whence our word for any maker's crowning achievement.
The double command at the heart of alchemical method: break the matter down to its principles, then bind it up again into a nobler form.
The formless base of the Work, held to underlie all bodies and to be recoverable from the meanest of them — Aristotle's materia prima put into the crucible.
The fifth substance beyond the four elements, which John of Rupescissa first proposed to distil from matter as its purest virtue, a programme carried on by the pseudo-Lullian corpu
The agent of transmutation and medicine of metals and men, end of the whole Work; the texts insist it is lapis et non lapis, a stone and not a stone.
The first stage of the Work, the putrefaction and death of the matter; revived by Jung as a figure for the dark opening of psychological transformation.
The washing and whitening that follows the black stage, figured as the moon, silver, or the white queen.
The yellowing stage between white and red, already dropping out of many texts by the fifteenth century — the reason later authors count three stages rather than four.
The reddening in which the Work is perfected, figured as the sun, gold, and the red king.
The union of opposed principles — sulphur and mercury, king and queen — pictured as a chemical wedding, and the pivot of the Rosarium philosophorum's emblem series.
Paracelsus' three principles — sal, sulphur, mercurius — the body, soul and spirit of every compound thing.
The slow digesting furnace of the Work; the word is honest Arabic, at-tannūr, 'the oven', naturalised into Latin alchemy through the twelfth-century translations.
The artificial man that Paracelsian writing claimed could be generated in a sealed vessel — the most notorious legacy of the De natura rerum attributed to Paracelsus.
The short Hermetic text, Arabic in origin and Latin from the twelfth century, whose dozen gnomic lines became the charter of Western alchemy.

The curse tablet of Roman magic: a leaf of lead inscribed, folded, pierced with a nail and sunk in a grave or well to bind a rival over to the powers below.

ox (ʾālep) — First of the row and numeral of the monad, alpha is yoked to omega in Revelation's 'I am the Alpha and the Omega', the standing cipher of beginning and end.
house (bēt) — As numeral of the dyad it marked the first departure from unity, which the Pythagoreans accounted the root of multiplicity and strife.
camel or throwing-stick (gīml; disputed) — Its numeral three is the triad which, Aristotle reports in De Caelo, the Pythagoreans held to be the first complete number, having beginn
door (dālet) — Numeral of the tetrad that closes the tetraktys (1+2+3+4=10), the triangular figure by which Pythagoreans swore — and itself a triangle in form.
window or jubilant figure (hē; disputed) — A great epsilon hung at Delphi beside 'Know thyself', and Plutarch devoted an entire dialogue, De E apud Delphos, to weighing what it mig
weapon, axe (zayin) — Its value is seven, not six, because the ghost of vanished digamma kept the sixth place in the numeral row.
fence, courtyard wall (ḥēt) — Bearing the value eight, it lent its number to the Ogdoad, the sphere of rest above the seven planetary heavens in Gnostic and Hermetic ascent.
wheel (ṭēt; identification uncertain) — The theta nigrum, initial of θάνατος ('death'), marked the dead on Greek and Roman lists — the letter men feared to see drawn against a name
hand, arm (yōd) — The least stroke of the alphabet — 'not one iota shall pass' (Matthew 5:18) — yet numerically the perfect ten of the Pythagorean decad.
palm of the hand (kap) — In the letter-oracles carved in Roman-era southern Anatolia every letter, kappa among them, answered inquirers with its own verse — divination by alphabet.
ox-goad (lāmed) — Ancient Platonists arranged the Timaeus world-soul numbers 1, 2, 4, 8 and 1, 3, 9, 27 along its two strokes — the 'Platonic lambda'.
water (mēm) — In Greek arithmetical notation a capital mu, for μυριάς, denoted the myriad — ten thousand — with its multiplier perched above it.
fish or serpent (nūn) — Its Phoenician parent nūn named a fish, an emblem the Greek world would meet again in the ΙΧΘΥΣ acrostic of the early Christians.
pillar or support (sāmek; disputed) — Xi stands at the centre of χξϛʹ, the three-letter numeral by which Revelation 13:18 writes 666, the number of the beast.
eye (ʿayin) — The 'small o' whose numeral 70 named the Septuagint's translators, cited in Greek simply as οἱ Οʹ, 'the Seventy'.
mouth (pē) — Initial of πατήρ, 'Father', contracted in early Christian manuscripts to the overlined nomen sacrum ΠΗΡ.
head (rēš) — Crossed with chi it forms the Chi-Rho monogram of Χριστός that Constantine, after his vision, set upon the labarum.
tooth (šīn) — Alone in keeping a special word-final shape (ς), while its lunate form Ϲ writes the ΙϹ ΧϹ of the icons.
mark, cross-sign (tāw) — The Epistle of Barnabas reads Abraham's 318 men as ΤΙΗʹ — the cross (Τ, 300) joined to Jesus (ΙΗ, 18) — perhaps the earliest Christian isopsephy.
hook, peg (wāw) — The 'Pythagorean letter': antiquity read its fork as the parting of the two roads, virtue and vice.
A pure Greek invention without Semitic parent; its modern election (in honour of Phidias) to name the golden ratio is a twentieth-century coda to letter-lore.
Plato's demiurge bends the world-soul's two bands 'in the figure of the letter Χ' (Timaeus 36b), which Justin Martyr took for a pagan glimpse of the cross.
Initial of ψυχή, 'soul' — whence its modern service as the sign of the psyche — and one of the last letters added to the alphabet.
Numeral 800 and terminus of the row; the Marcosian Gnostics prized the dove, περιστερά, whose letters sum to 801 — the very total of alpha and omega.
hook, peg (wāw) — Dead as a sound in most classical dialects, it survived as the numeral 6, later written with the ligature stigma (ϛ) — the third character of the beast's χξϛʹ.

Fullness — Valentinian Gnosticism (Nag Hammadi texts; Irenaeus' reports)

The Existing One — Septuagint, Exodus 3:14; Orthodox iconography

Not information but saving acquaintance: direct, experiential knowledge of divine things, the redeeming possession of the Gnostic.
The intuitive intellect that knows by immediate vision rather than reasoning; in Plotinus, the second hypostasis contemplating the One.
Breath as spirit: the Stoics' fiery world-substrate, the medium of oracles, and the divine element in man.
The soul, whose descent into body and destined return frame the whole Platonic religion of late antiquity.
Wisdom, at once a philosophical goal and, hypostasized, the aeon whose fall the Gnostics made the pivot of cosmic history.
Word, ratio, and ordering reason — the articulate structure of reality and the divine speech that utters it.
'God-working': the Iamblichean ritual art by which divine power acts through rites and symbols where argument cannot reach.
Union with the One beyond knowledge, the terminus of the Neoplatonic ascent.
The restitution of all things to their beginning — the Stoics' cosmic return and Origen's hope that even the last shall be regathered.
One of the planetary powers garrisoning the spheres, whose toll-gates the knowing soul must pass on its ascent.
An age or eternity — and, in the Gnostic plural, the living emanations that populate the divine Fullness.
The Fullness: the completed world of aeons that is the true, unfallen creation.
The Emptiness: the deficient region outside the Pleroma where shadow and matter subsist.
The 'public craftsman' who fashions the cosmos after a model — benevolent in Plato, blind in the Gnostic retelling.
Plato's teaching that learning is the soul's remembering of realities beheld before birth.
Purification of body and soul, the indispensable threshold of initiation and of philosophy alike.
A 'standing outside' oneself: the rapture in which, Plotinus says, the soul is alone with the Alone.
That about which the lips are closed (μύειν): the secret rite, and by extension the secret truth, of the initiated.

One of the ten emanations or vessels through which Ein Sof unfolds into manifestation, arrayed by the kabbalists as the Tree of Life.
The Godhead beyond all attribute and limit, prior to the sefirot and sustaining them.

The divine Presence dwelling within creation and accompanying Israel in exile, identified in kabbalah with Malkhut.
The lowest of the soul's grades, the animating life shared with all flesh (Genesis 2:7; Leviticus 17:11).
The middle grade of soul, seat of emotion and moral stirring, as the ruach of God moves over the waters in Genesis 1:2.
The higher, intellective soul breathed into Adam (Genesis 2:7), which kabbalah roots in Binah.
The fourth of the five soul-grades, a life-force that hovers above the body rather than dwelling within it.
The innermost grade of soul, the point of undivided union between the soul and God.
The mending of creation — in Lurianic kabbalah the raising of the scattered sparks to restore what the breaking of the vessels undid.
The soul's attachment to God (Deuteronomy 4:4), raised by Hasidism to the crown of the religious life.

Interpretation by number: since every Hebrew letter is also a numeral, words of equal sum are held to hint at kindred meanings.
Exegesis by acronym, reading a word as the initials of a phrase or unfolding a phrase from a word's letters.
Interpretation by systematic substitution of letters, as in the atbash cipher by which Jeremiah 25:26 writes Babel as Sheshakh.
The directed attention that turns prayer and mitzvah from performance into encounter; in kabbalah, meditative intentions keyed to the divine Names.
The shells of impurity that encase the holy sparks after the breaking of the vessels, awaiting their release.
The primal medium of emanation; kabbalah speaks of the or ein sof, the infinite light that precedes and fills all vessels.
The uniting knowledge of Chokhmah and Binah, counted by some schools as a quasi-sefirah on the middle pillar of the Tree.
The revolution of souls through successive lives for the sake of their tikkun, elaborated above all in Lurianic kabbalah.
The just man who is 'an everlasting foundation' (Proverbs 10:25); in Hasidism, the rebbe who binds his community to heaven.
The fragments of divine light lodged in all things, which the commandments are given to uplift and return.
The Lurianic catastrophe in which the vessels meant to hold the emanated light shattered, scattering sparks into the depths.
Scripture's tree of Eden and of wisdom (Proverbs 3:18), the kabbalists' name for the array of the ten sefirot, and the title of Chayyim Vital's great Lurianic compendium.
The masterwork of Castilian kabbalah, appearing in the late thirteenth century as a mystical midrash on the Torah.
The liturgical rite in which Israel joins the seraphic 'Holy, holy, holy' of Isaiah 6:3 — the Merkavah vision carried into daily prayer.

Read the alphabet right to left, tell apart the letters that deceive the eye, master the five final forms, and know honestly what hand the Torah scroll is written in.
Read the six vowel points you will meet most often, recognise the dagesh, and understand why the Torah scroll carries none of them.
Understand the shoresh, work two roots through their derivatives, and see why every Hebrew dictionary — and every kabbalistic word-play — is organised by root.
Recognise the prefixes ha-, ve-, be-, le- and mi-, take the first word of the Torah apart, and meet the vav that turns a Hebrew verb into past narrative.

Reckon gematria correctly on real cases, and know honestly what the several methods are and what the technique can and cannot claim.

Gardiner G1 — The alef, a weak consonant conventionally taken as a glottal stop — though its earliest value may have been an r-like liquid — opens the Egyptological sign order, and
Gardiner M17 — The yod-like weak consonant; a single reed leaf also writes the interjection 'O' and begins many divine names.
Gardiner M17a — The doubled reed writes final and dual y, a role also filled interchangeably by the two oblique strokes of Gardiner Z4.
Gardiner D36 — The ayin, a voiced pharyngeal like Arabic ʿayn, with no true English equivalent — hence the classroom compromise of a deepened 'ah'.
Gardiner G43 — A semivowel of enormous frequency, marking masculine plurals and countless word-endings.
Gardiner D58 — A stable labial stop throughout the language's history.
Gardiner Q3 — The plain square writes p, as in pr, 'house' — one of the first words every student reads.
Gardiner I9 — Besides writing f, the viper serves as the suffix pronoun 'he, his' — one of the busiest signs in any text.
Gardiner G17 — The owl, drawn face-forward unlike most birds, alone writes the preposition m, 'in, from, as'.
Gardiner N35 — Alone it writes the preposition n, 'to, for'; tripled, it writes 'water' itself.
Gardiner D21 — Also the preposition r, 'to, at, against', and the word for 'mouth' and 'utterance'.
Gardiner O4 — The lighter of Egyptian's two h-sounds, pronounced as in English.
Gardiner V28 — An unvoiced pharyngeal fricative, the ḥ of Arabic Muḥammad, distinct to Egyptian ears from plain h though English merges them.
Gardiner Aa1 — Gardiner filed this circle among his 'unclassified' signs because what it depicts is genuinely unknown; its sound is the harsh velar fricative of loch.

records.d: Gardiner F32 — The softer palatal partner of ḫ, and the word ẖt, 'belly, body', writes itself with this sign.
Gardiner O34 — Old Egyptian distinguished z from s, but the two sounds had merged by Middle Egyptian, leaving bolt and cloth interchangeable in writing.
Gardiner S29 — The commoner of the two s-signs, and the causative prefix that turns verbs transitive.
Gardiner N37 — The rectangular basin writes the sh-sound and the word š, 'pool, lake'.
Gardiner N29 — A uvular stop like Arabic qāf, also transliterated ḳ in older literature.
Gardiner V31 — Besides plain k, the basket writes the suffix pronoun 'you, your' (masculine).
Gardiner W11 — The pot-stand supplies the hard g, always as in 'gate', never as in 'gem'.
Gardiner X1 — The small loaf writes t and, tirelessly, the feminine ending -t of nouns and names.
Gardiner V13 — A palatalised t that in later Egyptian often relaxed back to plain t, so the two signs interchange in some words.
Gardiner D46 — The hand writes d; Egyptian's own word for the hand, ḏrt, begins instead with the palatal ḏ.
Gardiner I10 — A palatalised d, heard in the familiar renderings 'djed' and 'Djoser'; like ṯ it often weakened to d over time.
'Sun' — the god's name is the ordinary Egyptian word for the sun — The solar creator, supreme at Heliopolis (Egyptian Iunu), who crosses the sky by day and the Duat by night
A name written with two signs, throne and eye, that will bear several grammatical parsings at once, with no way of testing any of them against a pronunciation the script never reco
A name that almost certainly says 'throne', whose difficulty is not the sense but an initial consonant that the ordinary word for 'seat' does not supply and the hieroglyphs never w
A name whose ending tells us plainly that it means 'the one of X', and whose whole difficulty is that X — a Delta town, a word for the ibis, or something now lost — cannot be fixed
Usually connected with ḥr, 'the distant one' or 'he who is above' — Falcon of the sky and divine prototype of the king, worshipped at Hierakonpolis and Edfu
A name with three or four respectable candidate roots and no means of choosing between them, the god's duties being specific enough to make each of them look apt after the fact. —
A name that may well be the source of the verb usually cited to explain it, so that the etymology risks running backwards. — Craftsman-creator of Memphis who, in the Memphite Theol
'The Hidden One', from ı͗mn, 'to conceal' — God of Thebes who, fused with Ra as Amun-Ra, became 'king of the gods' of the New Kingdom empire
'Truth, right order' — the principle itself, personified as a goddess — Daughter of Ra, wearing the ostrich feather against which every heart is weighed in the Hall of Judgement
'The Powerful One', from sḫm, 'power, mastery' — Lioness daughter of Ra and consort of Ptah at Memphis, mistress at once of plague and of healing
'House of Horus' — a falcon enclosed within the hieroglyph of a walled estate — Goddess of love, music and the western necropolis, celebrated above all at Dendera
A name written phonetically with the water-pot and determined with the sky, so that the script supplies a suggestive sound and no secure sense. — The sky as a woman arched over the
A name whose own consonants shift from period to period, attached to an animal no zoologist has identified, each unknown having repeatedly been pressed into service to explain the
'He who comes into being', from ḫpr, 'to become' — The morning sun imagined as a scarab rolling its disc above the horizon, within Heliopolitan solar theology
The vital force created with each person and sustained after death by offerings, written with the sign of two upraised arms.
The mobile aspect of the person, pictured as a bird, free to leave the tomb by day and return to the body at night.
The transfigured, effective spirit of the blessed dead, attained through the rites of glorification (sꜣḫw) and often described as the union of ba and ka.
The name, itself a component of the person; to preserve a name in stone was to preserve its bearer, to erase it was a second death.
The heart as seat of mind, memory and conscience — the organ weighed against the feather of Ma'at.
The shadow, counted among the person's components and depicted, fittingly, by a sunshade.
Power or mastery as a divine and personal attribute, written with the sceptre of authority.
The dignified spiritual body of the mummified dead, ritually distinct from the corpse it perfects.
Truth, justice and cosmic order together — the condition the gods established and king and priest laboured to maintain.
Disorder, wrongdoing and chaos, the standing adversary of ma'at, marked in writing by the determinative of the small malignant bird.
The dark limitless water before creation, from which the first mound rose and into which the ordered world remains immersed.
The primeval mound-stone of Heliopolis on which the creator first stood, ancestor of obelisk and pyramid capstone alike.
The netherworld traversed nightly by the sun and after death by the justified, written with its own sign of a star within a circle.
'God' — any divine being — written with the cult flag that stood before every temple.
The creative power of effective word and rite, older than the gods who wield it, and itself divinised as the god Heka.
'Life' — the looped cross that gods extend to the nostrils of kings, the most recognisable of all Egyptian signs.
The pillar of stability associated with the backbone of Osiris, ritually raised erect at royal festivals.
'Protection', written with a looped herdsman's shelter, worn as an amulet and pronounced over mother and child.
The restored Eye of Horus, 'the sound one', emblem of healing and wholeness and the pattern for Egypt's commonest amulet.
'Dominion' — the animal-headed sceptre carried by gods and kings as the sign of rightful power.
The plumed white crown of Osiris, worn by the king in rites that joined him to the lord of the dead.
The rearing cobra at the royal brow, the fiery eye-goddess who strikes the king's enemies; the entry gives its logogram.
The 'House of Life', the temple scriptorium where sacred books were copied, guarded and taught.
The leopard-skin-clad officiant who performed the Opening of the Mouth, restoring the senses to mummy and statue.
'The god's words' — the Egyptians' own name for the hieroglyphs; the god-sign is written first by honorific transposition though read second.
'Servant of the god', the ordinary title of a temple priest, rendered by the Greeks as 'prophet'.
The 'answerer' figurine placed in the tomb to reply 'Here I am' when its owner is summoned to labour; earlier spellings šꜣbtı͗ and šwꜣbtı͗ also occur.
'Lord of life', the Egyptians' hopeful name for the sarcophagus, the chest from which the dead rise renewed.
The 'revered one', honoured in life by the king and provided for in death — the state every tomb inscription claims for its owner.
The force present before the world was divided: heka as cosmic energy, as a god in the sun's crew, and as the equipment issued to human beings for their defence.

records.d: Read the ḥtp-dı͗-nsw formula entire, clause by clause; know where such lines stood and what they were for; and know which parts of the standard translation are argued over.
Water; also the syllable /a/ — Its archaic form is two wavy strokes of running water, and it doubles as the commonest vowel syllabogram, supplying Akkadian scribes with their /a/.

records.s: du, gub, ĝen; Akkadian alāku, izuzzu
records.d: To go, to walk; to stand; to come — One sign for a family of related motions — du 'to go', gub 'to stand', ĝen 'to come' — from which the reader must choose.
Child, son, daughter; small — A single sign serves both tur, 'small', and dumu, 'child', and it opens the name of Dumuzi, the 'faithful son'.
House, household, temple — É is at once the physical house and the temple as an institution, so that the name of every great sanctuary begins with it: É.KUR at Nippur, É.SAG.ÍL at
Lord; the en-priest or priestess — EN is the lord and also the cultic office of the en, held at Uruk for Inanna and at Ur for Nanna, where from Sargon's reign onward the incumbent
Great, big, senior — It builds most of the great titles: lugal, 'king', is lú plus gal, 'big man', and Ereš-ki-gal is 'queen of the great earth'.
Wood, tree; determinative before wooden things — The classifier for anything made of wood — ploughs, thrones, weapons, the tamarisk of the incantations — and on its own the word fo
Ox, bull — The archaic form is a bull's head seen from the front, and the ox is among the units of wealth counted in the very earliest Uruk ledgers.
Eye; face, front, before — An eye drawn in profile; it also writes 'face' and 'in front of', and in the mathematical tablets igi marks the reciprocal of a number.
Wind, storm, rain; clay — Wind and storm, and also the clay of the tablet itself; written after the divine classifier it names the storm-god Iškur, read Adad.

records.s: ka, inim, dug₄, zú; Akkadian pû
records.d: Mouth; also word, to speak, tooth — One sign, many words — ka 'mouth', inim 'word', dug₄ 'to speak', zú 'tooth' — and the reader must judge from context, which is the central diffi
Earth, ground, place; determinative after place names — Written after a place-name as a silent determinative (Uruk^ki), and paired with AN in an-ki, 'heaven-and-earth', which is th
Pure, holy, bright; silver — Kù is 'pure' and 'holy' before it is 'silver', so that one word describes both a ritually cleansed space and the metal weighed out in payment as kù-bab
Mountain, foreign land, netherworld — The sign draws three peaks, and it means at once the eastern highlands, the foreign country and the land of the dead — geography and eschatolo
Man, person, human being — Set before an occupation it classifies the whole world of professions — LÚ.ḪAL the diviner, LÚ.MAŠ.MAŠ the exorcist — and the archaic sign is a standing
King — The word is lú plus gal, 'big man', and the writing is a single compound sign built of those two elements; Akkadian simply reads it šarru.
Divine office, ordinance, rite — The me are the fixed offices of civilisation, which Inanna carries off from Enki at Eridu in one of the best known of the Sumerian myths.
Name; year — Both 'name' and 'year', and mu lugal, 'by the king's name', is the formula by which oaths are sworn in Old Babylonian contracts.
Stone, bead, weight-stone; determinative before stone names — A determinative written before the name of any stone or bead, it heads the entries of Abnu šikinšu, the Babylonian han
Fate, destiny, allotted portion; abstract prefix — Prefixed to a noun it forms abstracts — nam-lugal 'kingship', nam-tìl 'life' — and standing alone it is the destiny decreed for a
Lady, mistress, queen — Unicode gives it a codepoint of its own, but on the tablets the lady is written with two signs, SAL.TÚG (𒊩𒌆), which is how Ninhursaĝa, Ninurta and Ereškig
Head; first, foremost, beginning — A human head in profile with the face marked, it gives Sumerian both 'head' and 'first', and in the Ur III ledgers saĝ-nita₂ and saĝ-munus count
Woman, female — It marks the female, standing before women's names, and combined with TÚG it writes NIN, 'lady'.
Brother — In ŠEŠ.UNUG it writes the city of Ur, and in ᵈŠEŠ.KI the moon-god Nanna who owned it.
Hand — The hand heads the diagnostic formula 'hand of the god' (ŠU DINGIR), by which a physician attributed an illness to the touch of a named deity.
Arrow; rib; to live — The sign is an arrow, and its readings run from ti 'rib' to tìl 'to live' — the pun on which Ninti, 'lady of the rib' and 'lady who makes live', turns in Enki
Ten; the corner wedge — With DIŠ it writes every number in the sexagesimal system, and so writes the sacred numbers of the gods in this hall — Anu's 60, Enlil's 50, Sîn's 30.
Sun, day, daylight, white — It shows the sun rising over the horizon, and serves as the logogram for the sun-god Utu, read Šamaš in Akkadian.
City, town, settlement — Placed before a city name in Akkadian texts it classifies the settlement, complementing the KI written after it in Sumerian usage.
Life, breath, throat; to rise — Zi is breath and life at once, Akkadian napištu, which takes the throat as the seat of living, and as a verb the same sign means 'to rise'.

records.l: Enlil (ᵈEN.LÍL; the second sign is KID, read líl)

'Lady of the Mountain' or 'Lady of the Foothills' — Mother goddess and shaper of mankind from clay; Keš and Adab
'Calf of the sun', from amar 'calf' and utu 'sun' — City god of Babylon raised to universal kingship; Esagila, with the ziggurat Etemenanki beside it
From the Semitic root nbʾ, 'to call, to name' — the announcer, or the one who is called; the same root gives Hebrew nābîʾ, 'prophet' — God of the stylus, of scribes and of the dest

The terrifying luminous aureole worn by gods, kings and sacred objects — visible, detachable, and capable of being stripped from a defeated god. It is paired with puluḫtu, the awe

The tutelary spirit that accompanies a person or guards a gate, addressed as a minor deity; the human-headed winged bulls and lions at Assyrian palace entrances are conventionally
The male counterpart of the lamassu, invoked in the pairing 'may a šēdu and a lamassu go at my side'; like her, it may also turn hostile. Transliterated here rather than written in
Originally a court official, a commissioner who attends a case; in magical texts a demon that lies in wait at thresholds and in dark places. Printed in transliteration.
The great anti-witchcraft series of eight tablets and a ritual tablet, performed through a single night, in which figurines of the sorcerer and sorceress are burnt as their power i
The companion series to Maqlû, addressed not to an outside sorcerer but to a sufferer under a curse or broken oath, whose offence is unknown and is therefore listed exhaustively un

The rubric written after an incantation to state what it is for — KA-inim-ma against a headache, against a ghost, for a sick eye. Conventionally cited in this transliterated form e
A statue or figurine, whether the great cult image of a god or the wax and clay effigy burnt in a rite; the same word covers both, since an image is understood to participate in wh
The residence within a temple precinct where the en-priestess lived, and the setting of the sacred marriage rite. Given here in transliteration: the Sumerian writing varies between
The 'seer', a trained specialist who put a question to Šamaš and Adad and read the answer in a sacrificed animal; his craft, bārûtu, was the most prestigious of the divinatory disc
From (w)âru, 'to instruct, to commission': the message returned by the gods through an examined liver, and by extension any instruction or commission. Given in transliteration.
Divination by inspection of the entrails, above all the sheep's liver, whose zones were mapped, modelled in clay for teaching, and read feature by feature. Transliterated here.
The canonical series of twenty-four tablets interpreting anomalous births of animals and humans as portents for the king and the land. Cited by its incipit, as Babylonian scholars
The great celestial omen series of some seventy tablets, covering the moon, sun, weather and stars, from which the scholars of the Assyrian court wrote their reports to the king. C
The ritual specialist who diagnosed the supernatural cause of an affliction and expelled it by incantation and rite, working explicitly as the deputy of Enki. His discipline, āšipū
The singer of the balaĝ and eršemma laments, whose office was to soothe the heart of an angry god, and who sang in the Sumerian dialect eme-sal. Transliterated here.
The senior cultic office of a temple, held as a rule by a person of the sex opposite to the deity served; at Ur the entu of Nanna was regularly a king's daughter.
The ruler of a city-state as steward of its god, a title deliberately more modest than lugal; Gudea of Lagaš styles himself ensi₂.
Literally 'big man', the standard title of a king, and the word rendered šarru in Akkadian. A ruler was lugal of a city, but only Enlil could make him lugal of the land.
The office of king considered as a thing in itself, one of the me, which the Sumerian King List describes as having descended from heaven and as passing from city to city with defe
The craft of the exorcist, its curriculum set out on a single tablet, and the great ritual series that curriculum names.
The conditional sentence as a scientific instrument, and the enormous series that collected the world's legible surface.
Seventy tablets of sky-omens, a network of watchers reporting to the Assyrian court, and the disputed rite by which a king was said to be removed from the path of an eclipse.
The Dream Book and its specialists, and the rites by which a bad dream was cancelled before it could take effect.
The formal architecture of the spoken rite: how an incantation declares its use, and by whose authority the man reciting it speaks.
The population of the invisible, illness as assault, and the diagnostic handbook that told an exorcist whose hand had struck.
A ritual that prescribed burying guardians beneath a house, and the excavated boxes in which archaeologists found what it prescribes.
The god as a resident to be fed and clothed, the ceremony that turned a manufactured statue into a living god, and the New Year at Babylon.
The profession of ritual weeping, the dialect it wept in, and the technologies of transfer by which impurity was moved out of a body.
The shape of the world as the scholars taught it: a corpse made into a sky, a freshwater deep beneath the ground, and a mountain that is also the country of the dead.

records.l: When On High — the Babylonian Epic of Creation
records.s: Enūma eliš · Anonymous. No ancient tradition names a poet. The poem is the achievement of the Marduk theology of Babylon, and the Assyrian recension copied at Ashur simply substitutes Aššur for Marduk throughout — an editorial act that tells us plainly how such a poem was owned.

A work of accretion that a named scholar gave its final shape.

records.s: Anonymous in both languages. The Sumerian poem survives on Old Babylonian school tablets, copied by pupils learning the scribal curriculum, which is how most Sumerian literature reaches us at all; the Akkadian poem is a first-millennium library text. Neither names a poet, and both plainly stand at the end of a long transmission.

records.s: Kabti-ilāni-Marduk, son of Dabibu, named in the poem's own closing section — one of the very few Akkadian works to identify its maker. The claim made there is not authorship but transmission: the god revealed the whole of it to him in the night, and when he recited it in the morning he left nothing out and added not one line of his own. Whether we read that as a formula or as testimony, it is a Mesopotamian poet's account of where a poem comes from.

records.l: The Exaltation of Inanna, with the Sumerian Temple Hymns
records.s: Enḫeduanna, daughter of Sargon of Akkad and en-priestess of the moon-god Nanna at Ur — commonly called the first named author in world literature, and named within the poems themselves. The attribution is genuinely disputed and must be reported as such. Enḫeduanna is beyond question historical: her calcite disc survives, and the seals of her servants. But every manuscript of these poems is an Old Babylonian school copy, some five centuries after her lifetime, and the ascription may be a later tradition fastening well-known works to a famous name. Reverence and scepticism have to be held together here; the case is strong and it is not closed.

records.s: Saggil-kīnam-ubbib, named by the poem itself and by no other means: the first sign of every line of each stanza spells out, stanza by stanza, an acrostic sentence declaring him an incantation-priest who blesses god and king. The recovery was gradual — Ebeling in 1926 could still read only fragments of the sentence, without the name — and the full reading came with later manuscripts. A Babylonian scholarly list appears to place a man of that name in the reign of Adad-apla-iddina, c. 1068–1047 BC. It is the surest authorial signature in Akkadian literature, and it is built into the shape of the poem rather than appended to it.

The Vedic sacrifice: the ordered offering into fire around which the ritual literature, and the earliest Indian speculation, is organised.
Revelation: the Veda as heard by the seers and held to be authorless and eternal, as against smṛti, 'that which was remembered', the tradition composed by men.

records.s: Ṛgveda · Anonymous ṛṣis of the Vedic clans. The hymns are ascribed by tradition to named seers and their lineages — Gṛtsamada, Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, Atri, Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha — and it is these families that give the six 'family books' (Maṇḍalas II–VII) their distinct character and internal ordering. The tradition does not regard the seers as authors: they are those who saw (√dṛś) what had no maker, the Veda being apauruṣeya, not of human origin. The arrangement into ten maṇḍalas, the fixing of the Śākala recension and the elaborate apparatus of recitation are the work of later redactors whose names are not preserved.

records.s: Mukhyopaniṣadaḥ · Anonymous and composite. The texts are staged as dialogue, and the speakers — Yājñavalkya, Uddālaka Āruṇi, Sanatkumāra, Naciketas, Śvetaketu, and the women Maitreyī and Gārgī Vācaknavī, who argue as sharply as any of the men — are literary presences as much as historical persons. Each Upaniṣad is affiliated to a Vedic school (śākhā) and stands at the end of a Brāhmaṇa or Āraṇyaka rather than free; the longer ones, Chāndogya and Bṛhadāraṇyaka in particular, are visibly stitched from earlier units of unequal age and idiom.

records.l: The Song of the Blessed One
records.s: Bhagavadgītā · Traditionally the work of Vyāsa (Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana), the legendary compiler of the Mahābhārata, the Vedas and the Purāṇas — a figure who functions in the tradition less as a person than as a principle of authorship, and to whom so much is attributed that single human authorship is not seriously maintainable. The Gītā is embedded in the Bhīṣma Parvan of the Mahābhārata, and is spoken by Kṛṣṇa to Arjuna but reported at two removes, by Saṃjaya to the blind king Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Scholars have long suspected the text of internal layering — a shorter Sāṃkhya-inflected core overlaid with theistic and Vedāntic material — though no reconstruction has won general assent.
records.d: Seven hundred verses spoken between two armies. Arjuna, seeing his kinsmen, teachers and friends arrayed against him, sets down his bow and refuses to fight; Kṛṣṇa's reply moves fr

records.s: Pātañjalayogasūtrāṇi · Patañjali — a name, and very little more. The tradition identifies him with the grammarian Patañjali who wrote the Mahābhāṣya in the second century BCE, and further with an incarnation of the serpent Śeṣa said to have fallen into the palms of a woman named Gonikā; philology supports neither identification. Philipp Maas has argued, on manuscript evidence, that the sūtras and the so-called Vyāsa-Bhāṣya are a single composition by a single hand, the Pātañjalayogaśāstra — which would make the 'commentary' not a later gloss but part of the work itself. The text is in any case largely a systematisation of practices and terminology already in circulation, some of it shared with Buddhist Abhidharma.

The Kārikā is explicitly a summary of an older and largely lost literature — the Ṣaṣṭitantra, the 'system of sixty topics', is named in it — so Īśvarakṛṣṇa is a redactor of an existing school rather than the founder of one. Kapila himself is a legendary figure, credited elsewhere with reducing the sons of Sagara to ash.

That internal debate tells strongly against single authorship of the whole in its present form. Tradition identifies Bādarāyaṇa with Vyāsa, and therefore with the author of the Mahābhārata and compiler of the Vedas; scholarship keeps them apart.

records.l: The Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra — Bhairava of Consciousness
records.s: Vijñānabhairavatantram · Anonymous. The text presents itself as an extract from the Rudrayāmala Tantra, a work largely lost and whose surviving portions are of doubtful relation to it; such framing is a standard device of Śaiva scriptural authorship and cannot be taken as a historical claim. It is cast as dialogue: the Goddess asks Bhairava what the ultimate reality is, having found the doctrines she has been taught insufficient, and his answer is the body of the text.

records.s: Śivasūtrāṇi · Vasugupta. The tradition holds that the sūtras were not composed but found: Śiva revealed their location to Vasugupta in a dream, and he discovered them inscribed on a rock — the Śaṅkarapāla — on the Mahādeva mountain near Śrīnagar, the rock turning over at his touch to show the text. Kṣemarāja, whose Vimarśinī is the standard commentary, reports this; other accounts make Vasugupta the recipient of an oral transmission. His disciple Kallaṭa is credited with the sūtras' dissemination.
records.d: The foundational text of the Trika, the non-dual Śaivism of Kashmir, and the counterweight in that tradition to the dualist Śaiva Siddhānta that preceded it in the valley. Its seve

records.s: Spandakārikāḥ · Genuinely disputed, and disputed since the ninth century rather than by modern scholarship. Kallaṭa, in his Vṛtti, presents the verses as his teacher Vasugupta's, and Kṣemarāja follows him; other authorities, including Bhāskara, make Kallaṭa himself the author and Vasugupta only the source of the doctrine. A third position holds that Vasugupta composed them as an exposition of the Śiva Sūtras. The question has never been settled and probably cannot be.

records.s: Tantrālokaḥ · Abhinavagupta — one of the few figures on this shelf who is unambiguously historical and unambiguously a single person. Philosopher, aesthetician, exegete and initiate in several lineages, he names his own teachers and his own parents in his works. The Tantrāloka is his summa. Jayaratha's thirteenth-century commentary, the Viveka, is effectively inseparable from it in transmission.
records.d: The most comprehensive treatment of non-dual Śaiva ritual, metaphysics and practice ever written, running to close to six thousand verses — some 5,859 — across thirty-seven āhnikas

records.l: The Glorification of the Goddess (Durgā Saptaśatī, Caṇḍī)
records.s: Devīmāhātmyam · Anonymous. The work is embedded in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa but is widely held to be an interpolation into it, and it circulates independently as often as within it. The narrative frame is doubled: the sage Mārkaṇḍeya relates to Krauṣṭuki how the sage Medhas told the deposed king Suratha and the cheated merchant Samādhi — both stripped of everything and both still unable to stop caring — the three stories of the Goddess.
records.d: Seven hundred verses — hence Durgā Saptaśatī, 'the seven hundred to Durgā' — and the first Sanskrit text to treat the Goddess not as a consort or an aspect but as the supreme reali

records.s: Haṭhayogapradīpikā · Svātmārāma, called Svātmārāma Yogīndra, about whom nothing is securely known. The work is openly a compilation: it names its authorities in a lineage running from Ādinātha through Matsyendranātha and Gorakṣanātha and some thirty other siddhas, and modern text-critical work has traced the majority of its verses to identifiable earlier sources — the Dattātreyayogaśāstra, the Vivekamārtaṇḍa (Gorakṣaśataka), the Amṛtasiddhi, the Śiva Saṃhitā, the Khecarīvidyā and others. Svātmārāma is thus an anthologist of genius rather than an author, and the text's coherence is his contribution.

records.s: Śrīmadbhāgavatapurāṇam · Traditionally Vyāsa, said to have composed it in his old age when the compilation of the Vedas and the Mahābhārata had left him unsatisfied, and to have taught it to his son Śuka, who recites it to King Parīkṣit in the seven days before Parīkṣit's death — the narrative frame of the whole. Scholarship treats the author as anonymous and the provenance as South Indian: the work knows the Tamil Āḻvār poet-saints and the geography of the Tamil country. Its Sanskrit is deliberately archaised in a Vedic direction and is unusually consistent across all twelve books, which has led several scholars to argue for a single hand rather than the accretive growth typical of purāṇas.

A door or gate; in the mystical writers the recurrent figure for the threshold of the heart and of the heavenly places, and the word that names the great gates of the Temple and of
Light, radiance; with ḥeshshōkā it forms the governing pair of Syriac cosmology, and it is the medium of every Syriac account of knowledge, in which to see and to understand are on
Darkness; not a substance in Syriac orthodoxy but a privation, a distinction pressed hard by Ephrem in the Prose Refutations directed against Marcion, Bardaisan and Mani.
An account or narration; the standard term for a saint's Life and for a chronicle, the genre through which Syriac writers preserved the history of the eastern churches and much of
Theology sung rather than defined: Ephrem's symbols, the two grades of the Book of Steps, and the East Syriac science of stillness from Evagrius to Isaac of Nineveh.
The Watchers who do not sleep, the Enochic material and the Syriac counter-reading of Genesis 6, and the nine ranks of Dionysius entering world literature through a Syriac translat
Bardaisan's school on nature, fate and freedom; the astronomers of Qenneshre; and a church that condemned the Chaldeans while its libraries held the tables.
The Syriac alchemical corpus that Rubens Duval translated for Berthelot: a working scriptorium's shelf, and the bridge on which Zosimos crossed from Greek into Arabic.
Sergius of Reshaina putting Galen into Syriac, the Christian physicians of Gondishapur and Baghdad, and a Book of Medicines in which pharmacy and prayer share a page.
The charm codices Gollancz printed, the inverted bowls of Sasanian Mesopotamia, and a repertoire of protection shared across Jewish, Mandaean and Christian scribes.
The physical objects and their grammar: rolls worn on the body, bowls buried at thresholds, and a formulary built from precedent, adjuration and seal.
Pseudo-Methodius reading the Arab conquest as chastisement rather than refutation, the Cave of Treasures, Alexander's northern gate, and the Last Emperor's long European afterlife.
Qenneshre, the Alexandrian curriculum in Syriac dress, Hermes enrolled among the witnesses to Christ, and the channel through which much of Greek thought reached Baghdad.

records.s: Mäṣḥafä Henok — the Book of Enoch
records.d: A book the whole world lost and one church kept: the five Enochic writings, complete in Geʿez alone until the Aramaic came up out of the Judaean desert.

records.s: Kəbrä Nägäśt — the Glory of Kings
records.d: The widest canon in Christendom, the books no one else kept, and the national epic that made a dynasty out of a queen's journey.
Four names carried by half a country, a commemoration in every month, and the two intercessors on whom Ethiopian devotion actually rests.
Spirits out of the giants, a demoness ridden down by a saint, an accusation that has done lasting harm, and a possession cult the church condemns and people go on attending.
A strip of parchment cut to the height of the body it defends, painted with eyes that stare back, and written with names that were never meant to be read as ordinary language.

records.s: Mäṣḥafä Ṭəbäb — the book of craft-wisdom
records.d: Recipe books in which a root, a prayer and the name of the disease are three parts of one prescription, and the man who wrote them was the same man who sang the office.

records.s: Täʾammərä Maryam — the Miracles of Mary
records.d: A book of miracles that works by being read, a covenant with terms, and a devotion that is not a department of Ethiopian Christianity but very nearly the whole of it.

records.s: mäftəḥe śəray — the loosing of enchantment
records.d: Binding and loosing as a technical vocabulary, the divine names as the instrument, and the holy water where people still go and still stay.

records.s: Bahrä Ḥasab — the sea of reckoning
records.d: A schematic year dictated by an archangel, thirteen months that still govern a country's business, and the divinatory manual that travels in the same codex as the computus.

records.l: The Classic of the Way and Its Power
records.s: Dàodé jīng · Attributed to 老子 Lǎozǐ (Lao Tzu), 'the Old Master' — a name that is a title rather than a name. The earliest biography, in Sima Qian's Shiji (c. 100 BCE), is already an admission of ignorance: it offers Li Er 李耳, styled Lao Dan 老聃, an archivist of Zhou whom Confucius is said to have consulted; then Lao Laizi 老萊子, a contemporary of Confucius who also wrote a book; then the Grand Scribe Dan 太史儋, who lived a century and a half later. Sima Qian declines to decide. The text itself names no one, and its rhymed, aphoristic, frequently self-contradicting surface reads as an accretion of sayings rather than the work of one hand.

records.s: Zhuāngzǐ · 莊周 Zhuāng Zhōu (Chuang Chou), conventionally c. 369–286 BCE, of whom almost nothing is known beyond a short and partly anecdotal Shiji notice placing him as a minor official at Meng in the state of Song. The seven Inner Chapters (內篇) are generally accepted as substantially his; the fifteen Outer (外篇) and eleven Miscellaneous (雜篇) are the work of later writers of several distinct persuasions, which A. C. Graham influentially sorted into a Primitivist, a Yangist and a Syncretist stratum. The book as we have it is a school, not a man.

records.s: Yìjīng · Anonymous and stratified. Tradition assigns the eight trigrams to the culture-hero Fu Xi 伏羲, the sixty-four hexagrams and their judgements to King Wen of Zhou 周文王 while imprisoned by the last Shang king, the line statements to his son the Duke of Zhou 周公, and the Ten Wings to Confucius. None of these attributions can be sustained on the evidence, though each mattered to the age that made it: the Wings are demonstrably of several hands and several centuries, and the Great Treatise contains material that cannot be pre-Han. The core text — the 周易 Zhōu Yì proper, judgements and line statements — is anonymous divination literature.

records.s: Tàipíng jīng · Anonymous, and presented as revealed rather than composed: the bulk of the text is dialogue in which a Celestial Master 天師 answers questions put by disciples called 真人, the Perfected. The Hou Han shu reports that one Gong Chong 宮崇 presented at court, in the reign of Emperor Shun (126–144), a book in 170 juan called the Taiping qingling shu 太平清領書 which his master Gan Ji 干吉 (also written Yu Ji 于吉) had received beside a spring. The Han shu records an earlier and separate attempt, by Gan Zhongke 甘忠可 under Emperor Cheng, to present a Taiping scripture of his own; he was imprisoned for it and died there. Whether any of these books is the ancestor of the surviving text is unresolved. Ge Hong's catalogue of about 320 lists a 太平經 in fifty juan, which is neither the 170 of the Hou Han shu notice nor the 57 that now survive.

records.l: The Wondrous Scripture of the Upper Chapters on the Limitless Salvation of Humankind, of Primordial Beginning
records.s: Yuánshǐ wúliàng dùrén shàngpǐn miàojīng · Presented as the speech of 元始天尊 Yuánshǐ Tiānzūn, the Celestial Worthy of Primordial Beginning, at the dawn of a cosmic cycle — the 元始 standing at the head of the title is that deity's name, not a description of the book. Its human origin is placed by Tang and later sources with 葛巢甫 Gě Cháofǔ, a kinsman of Ge Hong usually described as his grandnephew, who between roughly 397 and 402 produced the first Lingbao 靈寶 scriptures and back-dated their transmission to his ancestor Ge Xuan 葛玄. The scripture's own account of itself, in which it is recited ten times before an assembly of gods and the deaf hear and the blind see, is the only account it offers.

records.l: The Authentic Scripture of the Great Cavern, of Highest Clarity
records.s: Shàngqīng dàdòng zhēnjīng · Revealed, not written. Between 364 and 370 CE at Jurong, south-east of the Jin capital, the medium 楊羲 Yáng Xī (330–386) received nocturnal visitations from perfected beings — among them 魏華存 Wèi Huácún (252–334), a Celestial Master libationer become the Lady of the Southern Peak — and wrote down what they dictated for his patrons 許謐 Xǔ Mì and his son 許翽 Xǔ Huì. The Dadong zhenjing is the highest of the scriptures so received. A century and a half later 陶弘景 Táo Hóngjǐng (456–536) hunted down the surviving autographs, authenticated them by handwriting, and edited the corpus; his 真誥 Zhēngào is the record of that work and one of the most extraordinary documents in Chinese religious history.

records.l: The Scripture of the Yellow Court
records.s: Huángtíng jīng · Anonymous. The Inner Effulgences text is ascribed within the Shangqing tradition to revelation through 魏華存 Wèi Huácún, and it circulates in that milieu from the late fourth century; the Outer Effulgences text is earlier and unattached to any name. The calligraphic tradition attaches the scripture to 王羲之 Wáng Xīzhī (303–361), whose transcription of it survives in rubbings; the famous anecdote of the calligrapher who copied a Daoist scripture in exchange for a flock of geese is told of the Daode jing in the Jin shu, and only migrated to the Huangting jing in later retellings.

records.l: The Inner Canon of the Yellow Thearch
records.s: Huángdì nèijīng · Anonymous and multiple, framed as dialogue: the Yellow Thearch 黃帝 questions his minister 岐伯 Qíbó, and sometimes Bo Gao or Lei Gong, on the constitution of the body and the causes of illness. The attribution to Huangdi is a genre convention of the late Warring States and Han, by which technical knowledge was given a mythical warrant; nobody in the tradition has ever taken it as a claim about authorship in our sense.

records.s: Bàopǔzǐ · 葛洪 Gě Hóng (283–343), styled Zhichuan 稚川, of a southern gentry family at Jurong; Baopuzi, 'he who embraces the uncarved block', is the sobriquet he gives himself throughout. He is one of the very few authors on this shelf who is a person, with a career, a temper and a signed autobiographical postface. He names his teacher Zheng Yin 鄭隱 and his great-uncle Ge Xuan 葛玄, from whom he claims the Taiqing 太清 alchemical scriptures descended, and he complains at length about the credulity, avarice and incompetence of his contemporaries.

records.s: Zhōuyì cāntóngqì · Attributed to 魏伯陽 Wèi Bóyáng (Wei Po-yang), of whom nothing is known outside Ge Hong's Shenxian zhuan, where he appears as an adept of Wu who tested an elixir on a dog. Matter appended to the text names two further figures, 徐從事 Xu Congshi and 淳于叔通 Chunyu Shutong, as having had a hand in it, and the tradition has never been able to decide whether these are collaborators, transmitters or fictions. The 'three' of the title are variously explained as the Changes, the Huang-Lao teaching and the work of the furnace; or as three men; or as the three agents of the process. The book does not say.

records.s: Wùzhēn piān · 張伯端 Zhāng Bóduān (Chang Po-tuan, c. 984–1082), styled Pingshu 平叔 and known as 紫陽真人 the Perfected of Purple Yang; a minor official of Tiantai in Zhejiang. He states in his own preface that he received the teaching from a master at Chengdu in 1069 after a lifetime of fruitless searching, and does not name him; the commentators do not agree on who he was, one of them calling him only the Elder of Qingcheng, while later tradition identified him with Liu Haichan 劉海蟾 and made Zhang the first of the Five Patriarchs of the Southern Lineage 南宗. That lineage was articulated by writers of the following centuries, and is a claim about spiritual descent rather than a documented succession; it is recorded here as the tradition's own account of itself.

records.l: The Yellow Thearch's Scripture of the Hidden Tally
records.s: Huángdì yīnfú jīng · Attributed to the Yellow Thearch, which is to say anonymous. Its appearance in history is the work of 李筌 Lǐ Quán (fl. mid-eighth century), a military writer and Daoist who claimed to have found the scripture walled up in a stone chamber at Mount Song — the canon still styles him 少室山李筌, Li Quan of Shaoshi, after the peak in question — and who supplied it with the first commentary. Most scholars regard the text as a Tang composition, and a good many regard Li Quan himself as its author; a minority argue for a sixth-century date on the strength of its vocabulary. There is no manuscript or citation before Li Quan.

He is a compiler, not an author: the book is quotation throughout, from some seven hundred earlier works, and Zhang's contribution is the selection, the arrangement and a preface.
